title: Position-dependent friction in protein folding from a GLE derived with a non-stationary localized projection distribution
authors: Salma Salem, Lucas Tepper, Benjamin J. A. Héry, Henrik Kiefer, David D. Girardier, Roland R. Netz
abstract: The Generalized Langevin Equation (GLE) is an integro-differential equation of motion for a general observable of a many-body system and is rigorously derived using the projection operator formalism. In the standard derivation, a stationary canonical phase space distribution is used for the projection. Here, we derive a novel class of GLEs using a non-stationary projection distribution that constrains the initial ensemble to a hypersurface in phase space on which the observable has a fixed value $A_0$. As a result, all GLE parameters, and in particular the memory friction kernel, depend on $A_0$ and can be extracted from short simulations that do not sample the entire phase space. Applying this non-stationary GLE to protein folding trajectories, we find for villin and an $α$-helical poly-alanine segment that the total friction is higher in the folded state. These results demonstrate that observable-dependent friction effects are non-negligible and can be accounted for using non-stationary GLEs derived by constrained projection schemes.
summary: This work develops a novel Generalized Langevin Equation (GLE) framework by employing a non-stationary projection distribution, allowing friction parameters to depend on the observable's position. Applying this to protein folding, the authors find that position-dependent friction effects are significant, especially for larger proteins like villin, suggesting that standard, stationary models are insufficient for accurate dynamic description.
main_problem: The paper investigates the role of position-dependent friction effects in describing the complex dynamics of protein folding.
main_result: The study demonstrates that observable-dependent friction effects are non-negligible, particularly for proteins like villin, requiring the use of non-stationary Generalized Langevin Equations (GLEs).
method: The authors derive and apply a novel class of GLEs using a non-stationary projection distribution, constraining the initial ensemble to a hypersurface in phase space.
model_or_system: The system modeled is protein folding, using reduced models like poly-alanine and villin, whose dynamics are described by a Hamiltonian system and analyzed via the GLE.
key_observables: Constrained Mean Squared Displacements (CMSD), total friction ($\gamma$), and the memory friction kernel ($\Gamma$).
important_parameters: The initial constraint value ($A_0$), which dictates the position-dependent nature of the friction parameters.
main_assumptions: The standard GLE derivation assumes a stationary canonical distribution, which the authors overcome by using a non-stationary projection scheme.
figures_summary: Figures compare CMSD predictions from Molecular Dynamics (MD) versus the non-stationary GLE for Ala9 and villin, showing significant deviations for villin, and plot total friction vs. position $A_0$.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the GLE formalism, details the derivation using a non-stationary projection, applies this to protein folding trajectories (Ala9 and villin), and compares the resulting dynamics (CMSD and friction) against standard MD simulations.
why_interesting: The methodology of deriving dynamics from constrained, non-stationary ensembles is highly relevant to open quantum systems and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, providing a framework to incorporate system-specific constraints into generalized equations of motion.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Exemplary trajectory and free energy landscape of Ala9 (left) and villin (right). A/D contain segments of the MD simulation trajectories which show how the reaction coordinates change in time. B/E show the free energy landscape which is constructed from the position probability density of the trajectory using Eq. 1, with distinct states corresponding to free energy ”wells”. The colored lines run through the free energy minima; these values will be used for the time constrained MSD analysis. C/F illustrate the folding direction with respect to the reaction coordinate value from the unfolded to the folded state. Snapshots of two conformations are placed at their respective positions....

FIG. 2. Comparison between constrained mean squared displacement (MSD) obtained from molecular dynamics (MD) and generalized Langevin equation (GLE) simulations, using Eq. 2, for Ala9 (top) and villin (bottom). A/D show the memory kernels Γ(t) extracted from MD simulations and used to simulate the GLE. B/E show the constrained MSDs from MD trajec- tories. We can see that villin generally exhibits higher position dependence than Ala9. C/F show an individual comparison between the constrained MSDs from MD and GLE trajectories at specific A0 values. While for Ala9 the MD and GLE MSDs are in agreement, for villin significant deviation is seen in the folded and intermediate states.

FIG. 3. Position-dependent memory kernels of Ala9 (left) and villin (right) extracted from MD trajectories. A/C show a comparison of the extracted kernels. While the Ala9 kernels decay to zero, the villin kernels oscillate towards the end due to the shorter trajectory. B/D compare individual kernels with their fits. Ala9 kernels are fitted to a single exponential while villin kernels are fitted to a double exponential.

FIG. 4. Total friction γ of Ala9 and villin as a function of position A0, obtained from the integral over the kernel fits. For both proteins, γ increases towards the folded state. The increase is much more significant for villin (here large A0 cor- responds to the folded state), where γ in the folded state is about three times as high as γ in the unfolded state. The increase for Ala9 (here small A0 corresponds to the folded state) is only around 15%.

FIG. 5. Fit of the memory kernel components for Villin. We show three original components as blue dots and the two ex- trapolated short-memory components as orange dots. The lines represent the fitted geometric progression for γi and τi based on Eq. B3.
